Scroll is clamped to the last screenful, its height memoised per width and invalidated on every fold, and the event loop absorbs an input burst into one frame and survives a transient unreadable event instead of ending the session. Verified against the real 2,980-conversation index and a 168,000-notch stress harness across 7 pane sizes. 363 tests passing (317 at the start of this work), zero warnings.

title: Preview marking is eager, so the longest conversations cost 70-160ms to open
description:
Preview::load marks every drawn block up front. Cost is a function of conversation size, not of how much matched: highlight::spans is an fts5 insert per message, ~25us fixed plus ~60ns/byte.

MEASURED on the real index (2,980 conversations / 175,988 messages), worst single Preview::load per query: borrow checker 161ms, commits 145ms, learning 90ms, the 81ms, deep learning 81ms, cafe 70ms. The corpus's largest conversation is 1,479 drawn blocks / 942 KB. Distribution: median 6 drawn blocks, mean 38.5, and only 144 conversations (4.8%) over 200, 22 (0.7%) over 500, 1 over 1000. So the median selection is sub-millisecond and the tail blows the 30ms keystroke budget.

DO NOT 'fix' this by pre-filtering through fts_prose to find which messages match before marking them. That was tried and measured as a pessimisation: the TUI's final token is always a prefix, and fts5 cannot restrict a MATCH by conv_id, so it walks the whole posting list for the term across all 176k messages and filters afterwards. On the largest conversation, filter-then-mark measured 64ms for 'borrow checker', 242ms for 'commits' and 17.9 SECONDS for 'the', against a flat 110-126ms for marking everything. Predictable beat occasionally faster. A comment in preview.rs records this so it is not re-attempted.
design:
Lazy plus memoised is the shape that actually bounds it: the pane only ever shows ~36 rows, so mark a block the first time it is rendered and keep the result. Needs lines() to know the viewport — today it builds every line and lets Paragraph::scroll clip — and needs interior mutability on the block marks. The anchor is the wrinkle: it needs to know which block matched without marking all of them first.

The structural fix is chat-search-6eb.30 (external-content fts5), which removes the insert entirely and makes this free.
acceptance_criteria: Selecting the corpus's largest conversation repaints inside the 30ms keystroke budget; the measurements above are re-run and recorded.
notes:
MEASURED BREAKDOWN 2026-07-30, largest conversation in the corpus (1,468 drawn blocks, 942 KB), query "borrow checker", width 96, best of 3:

  SQL read + hydration   ~44 ms  (23%)   11.5 ms is the indexed query itself; the rest is
                                          allocating 942 KB of message text into Strings
  locating the marks    143.5 ms  (76%)   highlight::spans over the drawn blocks
  ratatui painting        1.6 ms  (<1%)   negligible
  ---------------------------------------
  Preview::load total   ~188 ms

Within the marking, per-MESSAGE overhead dominates per-BYTE cost roughly 3:1. Decisive
experiment - the identical 937 KB regrouped into fewer spans() calls:

  1468 calls: 224.3 ms      64 msgs/call ->   23 calls: 68.0 ms
   734 calls: 165.4 ms     256 msgs/call ->    6 calls: 59.0 ms
   367 calls: 135.1 ms    2048 msgs/call ->    1 call : 52.7 ms

So ~53 ms is genuinely proportional to text volume and ~170 ms is 1,468 scratch-table
round trips at ~117 us each. Cost tracks the NUMBER OF MESSAGES, not their size.

THIS CHANGES THE FIX. Batching is the cheap win and does not need the lazy/viewport
rework the design note proposed: feeding the scratch table once and reading marks back per
message would cut marking ~4x (144 ms -> ~35 ms) with no change to what is displayed and no
new invalidation rules. Lazy marking is still the ceiling, but batching gets most of it for
far less risk. chat-search-6eb.30 (external-content fts5) removes the insert entirely and
subsumes both.
close_reason:
Landed 2026-07-30 as ce6bee8. spans_many marks a whole conversation in one transaction and one query instead of one call per message. Load on the corpus longest conversation (1,468 drawn blocks, 942 KB): 188 ms -> 94 ms, with the marking portion going ~144 ms -> ~50 ms. The stress harness of 168,000 scroll notches went 17.6 s -> 6.1 s.

The design note on this bead proposed lazy/viewport marking; batching got most of the win for far less risk, so lazy marking was not needed. Two hazards handled: the delimiter pool is shared across a batch and so is drawn from the whole of C0 rather than six characters, and an exhausted pool falls back to per-message marking rather than costing the whole conversation its marks. Verified against the real index - 21,124 messages across five queries produced byte-identical marks either way.

The remaining open cost is now SQL read and hydration (~44 ms), not marking. chat-search-6eb.30 (external-content fts5) would remove the insert entirely.

title: Click a message header line to fold or unfold it
description:
click() (lib.rs:202) already handles the facet bar and the results body and does nothing for the preview; layout::scroll_target already hit-tests the pane; Preview::{focus, overrides, toggle_focused} already model the folds. The missing piece is a line-index -> block-index map.

Precedent is render::first_visible — shared between renderer and click handler with a comment saying that a disagreement selects the wrong row invisibly. Same move here: derive the map from the same rendered_rows() that lines() and follow_focus() use, so the three cannot drift.

Two hazards:

1. The offsets are already duplicated. lib.rs:142 hardcodes height-5 (border + 3 header lines + border) for the Alt-arrow viewport; render::preview builds those 3 header lines inline. A click needs row - inner.y + scroll - 3. Left as literals in two files, the click and the keyboard disagree the first time the header grows a line.

2. rendered_rows() and lines() agree only by luck: rendered_rows says 2 + text.lines().count() and lines() truncates rather than wraps, so one raw line is one row today. Add wrapping later and they diverge silently.

GLYPH COLLISION, worth fixing here: the results pane uses arrow-right/arrow-down for FOLD STATE (render.rs:227) while the preview uses arrow-right for FOCUS (preview.rs:231) — same glyph, two meanings, both on screen at once.
design:
Chevron carries fold state in both panes; focus is carried by STYLING that chevron (reverse video), so one column does double duty and it still reads on a monochrome terminal.

Click target: clicking a block's HEADER line — the collapsed one-liner, or the speaker line of an expanded block — toggles the fold and takes focus. Clicking a BODY line takes focus only. That way a collapsed line opens where you click it, a speaker line closes it, and clicking into body text does not collapse the block out from under you.
acceptance_criteria: Clicking a collapsed message expands it and clicking its speaker line collapses it again; clicking body text moves focus without folding; the mapping holds when the pane is scrolled and after the vertical reflow below SPLIT_MIN_WIDTH; keyboard and mouse agree on which message is which.
close_reason: Landed 2026-07-30. Highlighting now runs end to end: Hit carries snippet_spans (additive, ADR 12 intact), text::marked_runs/truncate_runs render styled runs truncated by display column, and the preview marks message bodies and collapsed lines from marks located once per (conversation, query) at load. Collapsed prose shows the line the query hit, so outline mode is a match map rather than a table of contents. The preview anchors on a matching message — from the marks, NOT Group::match_seqs, whose flat message positions cannot be resolved against the thread-contiguous order the pane draws in. sync_preview now keys on (conv_id, terms), which fixes marks going stale on a still-selected row as the query is edited. Clicking a message header line folds it, clicking body text only moves focus; the line->block map derives from the same rendered_rows the keyboard scrolls by, and PREVIEW_HEADER_LINES replaces the duplicated header offset. Fold chevron now carries fold state with focus as its style, resolving the collision where the results pane spent arrows on fold state and the preview spent one on focus. Verified end to end against a real 2,980-conversation / 175,988-message index: stemmed and prefix matches mark correctly. 347 tests passing (317 baseline), zero warnings. Remaining eager-marking cost is chat-search-me9.1.1.6.

title: cs init on a new machine silently omits 69% of the corpus
description:
`candidate_sources()` lists directories a running agent writes to, so it can never find `chatgpt-export` — that source is a manual export directory, hand-configured in ~/.config/chat-search/config.toml on this machine. There is nothing to detect.

The consequence is that `cs init` on a second machine writes a config that captures the agent sources and omits ChatGPT entirely. That is 2,011 of 2,935 conversations, 69% of the corpus, and nothing in the output says so.

This is the Capture epic's stated failure mode almost verbatim — 'every transcript-writing tool on the machine is either archived or reported as a present-but-unconfigured candidate; adopting a new agent cannot silently start a gap'. The gap here is not a tool that was adopted, it is a source that cannot be detected by the mechanism, which is worse because no future detection improvement will find it.

Found while correcting docs/ARCHITECTURE.md (chat-search-4ar.5).

Not the same as chat-search-a7k.10, which bounds how *stale* an existing export gets. This is about an export that was never configured at all.
design:
Detection is the wrong tool, so the fix is to say the thing rather than find it. Options: have `cs init` end with an explicit note that server-side sources exist and are not auto-detectable, listing them; or give the drift report from chat-search-a7k.12 a third category for known-undetectable sources that stays until configured or explicitly dismissed.

The second composes better — drift already runs every 300 s and already prints a paste-able config block, and a source that cannot be detected is exactly the case a one-time init message is worst at, because the person who needs it is the one skimming a first run.
acceptance_criteria: A fresh cs init, or the first archive run after it, states that ChatGPT and Claude.ai hold conversations that no detection can find and that they need an export. The statement names what fraction of a typical corpus that is. It does not repeat on every subsequent run.

title: Tombstones are read in five places and written in none
description:
ADR 9 says deletion keeps data and forgetting is explicit. `conversation.deleted_upstream_at` exists in the schema for it, `cs-core/src/search.rs` selects it in five places, `Group.deleted_upstream` carries it, and `cs search` renders a 'deleted upstream' tag from it.

Nothing ever sets it. Live index: 0 of 2,935 conversations, which is indistinguishable from 'nothing has vanished yet' and is why this survived unnoticed.

The information exists and is already captured — the archiver writes `vanished` events into the manifest (ADR 19). It simply never crosses into the index: no stage downstream of capture reads the manifest at all. So a conversation deleted from its source tool renders exactly like one still present, and the flag the CLI prints can never fire.

Found while correcting docs/ARCHITECTURE.md (chat-search-4ar.5), which claimed tombstones were built; the bead for that doc fix asserted the same thing. Both were wrong.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Archive a source, then delete a conversation from the live source directory.
2. `cs archive` records it as vanished in the manifest.
3. `cs index`, then `cs search` for it. It appears with no tombstone marking, identical to a conversation that is still upstream.
design:
The index is a pure function of the archive (ADR 1), so the writer belongs in the index build: read the manifest's vanished events for each source and set `deleted_upstream_at` on conversations whose source files are gone. That keeps the column derived rather than authored, which is what keeps it out of library.db (ADR 3).

Note the interaction with chat-search-a7k.20: an unmounted source currently reports every file as vanished. A tombstone writer reading those events would then tombstone the entire source. Fix the ordering — either a7k.20 first, or have the writer refuse a vanish event covering a whole source.
acceptance_criteria: A conversation whose source file is gone from the archive's manifest is marked, and cs search shows the tag it already renders. A source that is merely unreachable does not tombstone anything. Tombstoning is derived from the manifest on every index rebuild, never authored, so 'rm index.db && cs index' reproduces it exactly.

title: An unmounted or moved source records every file as vanished
description:
scan_source walks source.path; walk() swallows a failed read_dir and returns nothing, so every path the manifest still considers live is emitted as Change::Vanished. A source directory that is merely unreachable — external volume not mounted, laptop mid-restore, directory renamed — therefore writes a Vanished event per file, and on the next run the same files come back as Change::New (scan::tests::a_file_that_comes_back_is_new_again) and are re-captured in full.

Not data loss: the manifest is append-only and the archived bytes are untouched. It is a bogus event storm plus a full re-capture of the source.

a7k.12 now prints a 'missing' line for exactly this case, so the condition is at least visible. The fix is to distinguish 'directory is gone' from 'directory is empty' before emitting vanished events.
design: cs_archive::drift::detect already computes the missing set from one is_dir probe per configured source. Either skip the source in the archive loop when it is in drift.missing, or teach scan_source to return an error/empty scan when source.path is not a directory. Prefer the latter: it keeps the decision inside the crate that owns the walk, so cs scan gets it too.
acceptance_criteria: A configured source whose directory does not exist produces no Vanished events and no re-capture when it returns. cs scan and cs archive both report it as unreachable rather than as a source that lost every file.

title: No way to discover what can be filtered on
description:
From TUI feedback 2026-07-30: 'a reminder of the dsl syntax could be helpful. I couldn't remember how to filter by date or even what filters are available.'

Two distinct gaps behind that:

1. **There is no DSL yet.** chat-search-6eb.11 is blocked on chat-search-6eb.26, so date and project filtering do not exist to be remembered. Worth saying plainly in the UI rather than letting a user hunt for syntax that is not there.

2. **Even source filtering is unreachable from inside the TUI.** The facet bar renders but is not keyboard-drivable — Tab is bound to expand. So today the only filter is the one nobody can apply.

The affordances, in increasing cost:
- Search-box placeholder carries an example, the way fast-resume's does ('Search titles, messages, paths. Try agent:claude'). Free, and it is the first thing anyone reads.
- Live syntax highlighting in the input with invalid values struck through (docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §5) — ~70 lines, and it makes an undocumented DSL self-teaching.
- Ghost-text completion of filter values on Tab.
- A key-triggered help overlay listing every filter. Note the keymap constraint: unmodified keys belong to the search box, so this cannot be '?'.

Bind the facet bar to a key regardless of when the DSL lands — a filter that renders but cannot be applied is worse than one that is absent.
acceptance_criteria: A user who has never read the docs can discover, from inside the TUI, what can be filtered on. Source filtering is reachable by keyboard. Filters that do not exist yet are not implied by the UI.
notes:
CORRECTION 2026-07-31: gap 1 in the description — 'There is no DSL yet' — is no longer true. chat-search-6eb.11 landed, and its dependency on chat-search-6eb.26 had already been removed on 2026-07-30. agent:, dir: and date: all parse out of the query text and filter results, in the TUI as well as the CLI, through one parser.

That changes what this issue is for rather than closing it. The affordance list stands and gets *more* valuable, not less: there is now a real syntax to be unable to remember, which is exactly the feedback this was filed from. Specifically:

- The search-box placeholder can now name a filter that works.
- Live syntax highlighting has something to mark: Query::rejected() returns the tokens whose values select nothing (date:nope, a half-typed agent:), which is the fact the struck-through rendering in docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §5 needs. Both clients already print it as flat text; the ~70-line version is what makes it self-teaching.
- Ghost-text completion of agent: values can be driven from the facet counts the app already holds; date: values are a fixed list (today, yesterday, week, month, plus <Nu / >Nu with units m|h|d|w|mo|y).
- A help overlay now has a complete syntax to list.

Gap 2 (the facet bar is not keyboard-drivable) is untouched by 6eb.11 and remains as written. chat-search-me9.16 is the related cleanup: the facet bar should filter by rewriting the query text rather than keeping App.source beside it.

title: Set the TUI ranking limit, and record the warm keystroke numbers
description:
Measured 2026-07-30 in the TUI against the 293 MB / 172k-message index, release build:

| query | ms | query | ms |
|---|---|---|---|
| emb | 10 | deep | 332 |
| embe | 11 | deep l | 15 |
| embed | 11 | rus | 1193 |
| embedd | 8 | rust | 25 |

This is the revisit trigger recorded on chat-search-me9.1 when chat-search-me9.4 was closed: 'if any keystroke path measures over ~30 ms, the search is no longer synchronous.' It is over by 40x on 'rus'.

**Length is the wrong lever.** MIN_PREFIX_LEN exists on the theory that short prefixes are the expensive ones, and the measurements it cites (h* 2510ms, ho* 51ms, hov* 16ms) were taken on 40k prose messages. The corpus is now 172k. Cost tracks how many index terms the prefix expands to, not how many characters were typed: 'rus' at 3 chars costs 1193ms while 'rust' at 4 costs 25ms, and 'deep' at 4 chars costs 332ms. Raising the threshold would not have caught 'deep'.

Adding a second token collapses the cost ('deep' 332ms -> 'deep l' 15ms), because the intersection is evaluated before scoring.

The TUI now holds queries under MIN_PREFIX_LEN entirely (chat-search-me9.1), which removes the 1-2 char scans but does nothing for these.
design:
Options, none yet chosen:

A. Reopen chat-search-me9.4 — move the search off the event loop with generation numbering. Does not make the query faster; keeps the UI responsive while it runs, and is what the revisit trigger explicitly says to do rather than reinventing.

B. Bound the expansion. Consult fts5vocab for the term count a prefix would expand to and fall back to exact match past some ceiling. Turns an unbounded scan into a predictable one, at the cost of a lookup per keystroke and a result set that changes shape at the boundary.

C. Defer prefix expansion until the query stops changing — expand only when no keystroke has arrived for N ms. Keeps every completed query exact-fast and pays the prefix cost once. This is debounce, which the synchronous design deliberately avoided, and it only makes sense together with A.

D. Raise MIN_PREFIX_LEN. Cheapest, and demonstrably insufficient: 'deep' is four characters and costs 332ms.

Worth measuring first: how much of the 1193ms is BM25 scoring versus the fts5 prefix scan, since B only helps if it is the scan.
acceptance_criteria: p95 keystroke-to-render under 30 ms on the 172k-message index, measured across a set of prefixes chosen to include the expensive ones ('rus', 'deep', 'com', 'pro'), not only convenient ones. A query that cannot meet the budget degrades visibly rather than freezing the interface. The measurements are recorded so the next corpus growth can be checked against them.
notes:
CORRECTION 2026-07-30, after measuring properly. The headline numbers in the description (rus 1193ms, deep 332ms) were COLD-CACHE first-touch, not steady state. Re-measured warm, release build, limit=100:

  rus 47-72ms | deep 19-23ms | com 89-96ms | pro 246-443ms | embedding 16-64ms

First touch of any given term costs 700-1300ms on the 293 MB index; every repeat is an order of magnitude cheaper. So there are two separate problems wearing one number.

The fts5 scan is NOT the cost, which settles the question the design field asked to measure first: '"rus"*' matches 9,921 rows in 6ms and '"deep" "l"*' 922 rows in 35ms, timed inside a warm sqlite session. Option B (bounding the expansion via fts5vocab) therefore does not help — it optimises the part that is already fast.

Two remaining levers, both downstream of the scan:
- Cold page cache on a 293 MB file. A first-touch cost per term, paid once. Prefetch at startup, or accept it.
- The ranking ceiling, 'limit * 50' clamped to 500..5000. The TUI asks for limit=100, so it ranks 5,000 candidate messages to display ~35 rows. limit=40 roughly halves the broad-prefix cost (pro 443ms -> 64ms, rus 72ms -> 44ms). Cheapest available win and it is purely a client choice.

Partly overtaken: the widening bug fixed on 2026-07-30 (MIN_PREFIX_LEN applying to a multi-term query's final token) also cut these times, because a bounded intersection is cheaper than a lone prefix — 'deep learning' now costs 8ms at limit=100.
2026-08-01, from chat-search-6eb.38: the prefix index is measured and rejected (ADR 6),
which closes the last option that was about the fts5 scan. Both B ('bound the expansion')
and the prefix index optimise the part that was already fast.

What the measurement points at instead: the cost is bm25 scoring the whole match set.
'the'* ranks in 59.9 ms and 'the' — no prefix at all — ranks in 48.9 ms, so only 11 ms
of it was ever the expansion. search_grouped pulls a ceiling of limit*50 candidates and
ORDER BY bm25(...) has to score every one of the 37,911 matching rows before LIMIT can
discard them; stripped of the scoring the same query is 12 ms. So the levers left are
the ceiling, the scoring, or option A (get it off the event loop) — not the index.

Also worth knowing: cold first touch in a fresh process is a separate problem and no
index change touched it. pro 637 ms, the 487 ms cold against 30/60 ms warm. The TUI
pays that on its first keystroke every launch.

title: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md 'Current state' table is wrong in both directions
description:
Last synced 2026-07-28 and now misleading to anyone — human or agent — who reads it to decide what exists.

Says 'not built' or 'PoC only' for things that are built:
- Archive reader: listed 'not built'. crates/cs-archive/src/reader.rs exists and every importer reads through it.
- Importers Codex + Claude Code: listed 'PoC only, read live source dirs not the archive'. Both read the archive (ADR 1), and Gemini and ChatGPT export exist too, listed as 'not built'.
- Indexer + BM25: listed 'PoC only — flat messages, no DAG, no head_id, no tombstones'. All three exist.
- Clients: listed 'not built'. There is a CLI with grouped search and scripts/cs-fzf.

Also missing entirely, added 2026-07-30: ~/.chat-archive/queries.jsonl (chat-search-6eb.22). The flow diagram shows index.db as disposable and library.db as precious, and the query log is a third category the picture has no node for — precious, already real, and currently sitting beside the disposable one. Worth drawing, because it is the file whose loss actually costs something.
design: The doc says it is derived from the decision log the way index.db is derived from the archive. If that is meant literally, the fix is to regenerate rather than patch, and to decide how often. If it is aspirational, the honest move is a shorter doc that points at the code for current state and keeps only what the code cannot say.
acceptance_criteria: The 'Current state' table matches what is in crates/, or the section is removed in favour of something that cannot rot. The query log appears in the data-flow picture.
close_reason: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md rewritten 2026-07-30. The 'Current state' table was replaced rather than repaired, on the reasoning that a status table has no failure mode — nothing breaks when it goes stale and no test reads it. What exists is now delegated to commands whose output is the code; what is deliberately absent is kept as prose with a falsifying command per row, because an absence has no file to point at. Also corrected: the query log added to the data-flow diagram, an invented 'Export ingest' component deleted, rebuild time and cadence figures refreshed, ADR 14 moved out of open questions. Turned up three findings outside the doc: tombstones are never written (filed), chatgpt-export is undetectable by cs init, and .zst rollouts are captured but unreadable (chat-search-a7k.11).

title: Ranking eval harness: sheets, pooled candidates, metrics
description: Split out from chat-search-6eb.9 so a finished deliverable is not filed under a deferred one. That issue is 'build the ranking eval SET' and is deferred pending real queries; the machinery to score any set is done and in use.
design:
cs-core/src/eval.rs holds the arithmetic only — graded relevance 0-3, nDCG@k with exponential gain, MRR, success@1/@5, exact@1, pool coverage. No I/O, so it is unit-testable and linkable by any client.

crates/cs/src/eval.rs holds the client half: 'cs eval sheet' writes one gradeable file per query, 'cs eval collect' reads the grade column back, 'cs eval run' scores.

Decisions worth not relitigating:
- A file you edit, not an interactive prompt. Relevance is comparative — whether a result is a 2 or a 1 depends on what else came back — and a one-at-a-time prompt makes that call from memory. The prompt loop was built first and deleted (183 lines).
- Candidates are pooled from three rankers (default, decay=0, repeat_weight=0), because judging only what the shipping ranker returns is how a tuning run proves the shipping ranker optimal.
- Ordered newest-first with no rank shown: rank order would anchor the judgement to the ranking being measured, and would reshuffle a half-graded file on every re-emit.
- A query with no positive judgement is unscorable, not zero, so adding a query never lowers the score.
- Grade 1 is not a hit for MRR/success@k.
- REPEAT_WEIGHT and DECAY became per-query fields on Query so the pool can vary them and 6eb.13 is a shell loop. Two tests prove each actually moves the ranking, because a sweep over a dead knob reports a flat line that reads as 'the current value is fine'.
acceptance_criteria: cs eval sheet/collect/run work end to end against a rebuilt index; metrics are unit-tested; coverage, unscorable and dangling judgements are reported as reasons to distrust the numbers.
close_reason: Landed 2026-07-30. 170 tests green across the workspace; 11 metric tests in cs-core/src/eval.rs, 8 in crates/cs/src/eval.rs, 2 proving the tuning constants actually move the ranking. Verified end to end on the real 2,963-conversation index: 24 sheets, 263 candidates, round trip through collect and run, plus the overwrite and unknown-id guards.

title: Project as a search filter
description:
From the 2026-07-30 design discussion: date and project are the strongest cues for recognising which conversation was wanted, stronger than anything in the text.

That argues for filters rather than ranking weights. A filter is predictable, debuggable and obviously wrong when it is wrong; a ranking weight is a guess with a number attached that silently trades against everything else. Date filtering is already chat-search-6eb.11's job (after:/before:); project is its natural companion and has no bead.

Available now: 940 conversations carry cwd across 99 distinct values, so the agent third of the corpus can be filtered today. ChatGPT conversations have no cwd and would fall outside any such filter, which needs saying in the UI rather than looking like missing data.
design: cwd -> project name is a cheap derivation (basename, or nearest ancestor holding .git). Derived, so ADR 16 says it must never become part of an id. Pairs with chat-search-me9.14, the facet bar that has to show coverage state rather than just non-empty sources — 'project' is exactly a facet two thirds of the corpus cannot answer.
notes:
Measured 2026-07-30 against the real index, and both findings make the cheap derivation harder than the design line suggests.

1. Basename is lossy in a way that matters here. 100 distinct cwd values collapse to 90 distinct basenames, and the collisions are not harmless: i is the basename of SEVEN different directories, mars-attacks of three, i-2 and career of two each. A large share of Codex cwds are ~/Documents/Codex/<date>/<slugified-first-prompt>, which are per-conversation scratch directories rather than projects. Basename-as-project would produce a facet with seven unrelated entries called i.

2. The nearest-ancestor-holding-.git alternative breaks ADR 1. That walk reads the LIVE filesystem, so the column would not be a pure function of (archive, importer version): delete a repo and rm index.db && cs index yields different output. ADR 1 calls that corollary a bug rather than a chore. If the git-root derivation is wanted it has to be captured at IMPORT time from something in the archive, which is a larger piece of work than the design line implies.

This no longer blocks chat-search-6eb.11: dir: filters on cwd, which exists. See that issue for the measurement.
close_reason: Demolished by its own measurements. Basename collides (7 directories share 'i', a large share of Codex cwds are per-conversation scratch dirs); nearest-.git-ancestor reads the live filesystem and so breaks ADR 1. Meanwhile dir: filters on the existing cwd column with no derivation at all (see chat-search-6eb.11). What was left — a display NAME for the facet — belongs to chat-search-me9.14. If the git-root derivation is ever wanted it must be captured at import time from something in the archive, which is a different and larger bead than this one.

title: Show where matches fall in a conversation, not just how many
description:
A match count alone cannot answer 'is this conversation about my query'. Three hits bunched at the start of a forty-message conversation is the subject; three at the very end is an aside raised on the way out, and the two deserve different grades and different ranks.

Not hypothetical: 86 of 147 conversations over 15 turns span more than four hours, so most long ones are several sittings across more than one topic.
design:
Group gained msg_count, prose_count and match_seqs (every match's 0-based position, not just the nested ones — 'nested' would truncate the shape to three). cs_core::match_density renders a fixed ten-cell strip, in cs-core rather than per client for the same reason as ended_date: a second implementation is a second chance to bucket it differently.

Chosen over simply showing three snippets, which gets noisy when two of the three are unrelated.
acceptance_criteria: A result carries where its matches fall as well as how many. The strip is always ten cells regardless of input, including empty, out-of-range and zero-length conversations.
close_reason: Landed 2026-07-30 as part of the sheet work. Group carries msg_count/prose_count/match_seqs; cs_core::match_density renders the strip; the eval sheet shows 'N of M prose matched' plus the strip alongside one snippet. Two synthetic tests, including the subject-vs-aside distinction and fixed width on degenerate input. Visible payoff on real data: an RL-environment query returned 'Interview Prep with Ege' with strip ·▁······▁▁, which reads as a tangent at a glance.

title: Harvest the eval set from real searches
description:
Supersedes the hand-authored approach in chat-search-6eb.9, which stalled on a real problem: a query invented by reading the corpus has no information need behind it, so nothing is 'the one I meant' and most candidates grade as vaguely useful. Judging measured the queries, not the ranking.

Logging landed 2026-07-30 (chat-search-9zk). 'cs search' records query + result ids; 'cs pick' records which conversation was opened and at what rank; 'cs needs' folds the log into one row per distinct query.

The work here is the second half: turn an accumulated log into an eval set. A picked conversation is a grade-3 with nobody grading anything, and the queries are real needs in their real distribution.
design:
Wait for data before building. Roughly 50-100 picks across 20+ distinct queries is enough to be worth converting; below that the set is thinner than the 24 hand-written queries already seeded.

Conversion is mechanical: each Need becomes a [[query]] with q = the literal text, and each picked conv_id becomes an Exact judgement in the log. Feed the result straight into 'cs eval run'.

Keep the pooled sheet flow rather than replacing it. Click data has a known position bias — a conversation can only be picked if it was shown, so a good result the ranking buried never appears as an answer, and a harvested-only set would score the current ranking as perfect by construction. Pooled judging is what covers that hole, so the two compose: harvested queries say what to ask, pooled judging says what else was there.
acceptance_criteria: 'cs eval harvest' turns the query log into a set plus judgements that 'cs eval run' scores without further editing. Queries with no pick are carried across unjudged rather than dropped, since an abandoned search is a real need the ranking failed. The generated set is distinguishable from the hand-written one, so the two can be scored separately.

title: cs index reported conversation objects, not rows
description:
IndexStats.conversations incremented once per Conversation object write_one saw, but the table is keyed on conversation.id and upserts. Any conversation delivered twice was counted twice while only one row existed.

Two ways it bit on 2026-07-30:
- Two overlapping ChatGPT exports reported 4,022 conversations for an index holding 2,011. Dedup was correct; the number made it look broken, which is the expensive kind of wrong.
- The real corpus was reported as 3,032 when the index holds 2,963 — 69 conversations span several transcript files (ADR 7) and were each counted twice. That inflated figure had already reached docs/BACKLOG.md.

Fixed as part of chat-search-a7k.8: write_one asks whether the row exists before upserting (ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE reports one changed row either way, so it cannot be inferred afterwards) and increments either conversations or the new IndexStats.merged. 'cs index' prints the merged count when non-zero, and the JSON report carries it.
acceptance_criteria: IndexStats.conversations equals the row count in the conversation table. A conversation delivered twice increments merged, not conversations. Covered by a synthetic test.
notes: Closed on arrival — filed for the record because the wrong number was published in docs/BACKLOG.md and in a7k.8's reasoning before it was caught.
close_reason: Fixed in the same change that found it. write_one now asks whether the conversation row exists before upserting and increments IndexStats.conversations or the new IndexStats.merged accordingly; 'cs index' reports merged when non-zero. Synthetic test: a_re_delivered_snapshot_is_counted_as_merged_rather_than_as_a_second_conversation. Corpus figures in docs/BACKLOG.md corrected to 2,963.

title: Facet bar must show coverage state, not just non-empty sources
description:
A source with zero indexed conversations is invisible if the facet bar is built from the index alone — the failure fast-resume ships (tui/state.rs:278-286 keeps only count > 0). A configured source whose importer threw, or whose archive run never happened, then produces a chip row that looks complete. You search, get nothing, and conclude you used a different tool, when the truth is a broken importer.

The Capture epic explicitly forbids this: a source that is skipped says so; it never just fails to appear. The facet bar is the only place in any client where the full source inventory is visible, so it is where coverage state belongs.

Build the chip row from config union index, in three states:
- configured, has rows -> normal chip with count
- configured, zero rows -> dim chip, ! marker, count 0
- detected on machine but not configured -> distinct dim style, no count (chat-search-a7k.12)

Applies to the CLI's per-source table as much as the TUI.
design: See docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §4. The chip row is a projection of query state, so a dim zero-count chip must still be selectable — clicking or Tab-cycling onto it writes agent:<source> into the query and shows an empty result set with an explanation, which is the informative outcome. Depends on cs-core exposing configured-but-unindexed sources, not just indexed ones.
acceptance_criteria: A configured source with zero indexed rows renders as a dim chip with a zero count rather than being omitted. A source present on the machine but absent from config renders in a third style. Selecting a zero-count chip produces an explained empty state, not a silent blank list.

title: Report append delta, not whole-file size, in capture byte totals
description:
An append re-captures the whole file, and the capture report bills the whole file every
time. Replaying the real manifest: 146 `appended` events reported **1176.2 MB** under the
whole-file formula against **31.8 MB** of actual new bytes — a **37x** overstatement, median
append delta 75 KB against multi-MB files. Cumulatively across 1201 capture events the
report has claimed 3411.7 MB against a 2267.3 MB live archive.

chat-search-a7k.6 made the real marginal cost *visible* — `cloned_bytes` / `copied_bytes`
now read `0.0 MB new on disk` on this reflinking machine — but did not remove the error:
`apparent_bytes` and the headline `bytes` key still bill the entire file every 300 s. Note
that allocated blocks cannot fix this either; a7k.6 measured allocated/apparent at 1.0010
over the real archive, and an APFS clone reports the source's full `st_blocks`, so no
stat-based figure sees the sharing.

Cheap to do: both `size` and `prior.fingerprint.size` are already in hand at the capture
site, so the delta is a subtraction, not new plumbing.

Matters for two reasons beyond tidiness. On any non-reflink filesystem the re-copy is real
write amplification, not a reporting artifact. And ADR 20's revisit trigger is "measured
growth exceeds 1.5 GB/month" (DECISIONS.md:543) — chat-search-4ar.2 wants to mechanise
exactly that trigger, and feeding it a 37x-inflated number would fire it on re-counted bytes
rather than on real growth.
acceptance_criteria: The capture report distinguishes new bytes from re-captured bytes: an append of 75 KB to a 5 MB file reports ~75 KB of growth, not 5 MB. Replaying the existing manifest through the new formula yields a cumulative figure that tracks the 2267.3 MB live archive rather than 3411.7 MB. The month-over-month growth number that feeds ADR 20's 1.5 GB/month trigger (and chat-search-4ar.2) is computed from the delta, so the trigger cannot fire on re-counted bytes. Existing JSON keys keep their meaning, as in chat-search-a7k.6.

title: Confirm title-fold thread ordering over multi-thread conversations
description:
For conversation claude-code:8e4aee14, the index takes first_user from the main transcript while a path-sorted walk takes it from a subagent file — Rust's Path: Ord puts '<id>/subagents/...' before '<id>.jsonl'.

This is the exact shape of a silent-corruption bug already recorded as fixed in ADR 7 (docs/DECISIONS.md:117): 'Directory enumeration order is not guaranteed and differs between runtimes... With first-write-wins, 13 conversations took a subagent's opening line as their title instead of the real name.'

Observed incidentally by the agent fixing chat-search-n58.3, whose scratch harness disagreed with the index by exactly one conversation. May be a regression, may be an artifact of that harness's own ordering rather than the indexer's — unconfirmed either way, which is why this is worth a look rather than a fix.

ADR 7 calls this class out as silent corruption: the index looks fine and contains the wrong thing.
acceptance_criteria: Either a test pinning the indexer's COALESCE/first-write order across a multi-thread conversation, or a recorded confirmation that the observed difference was the harness and not the indexer.

title: Split ranking from hydration in search_grouped
description: search_grouped pulled up to 5000 candidate messages and built a snippet for every one, then discarded all but limit x nested. message.text is by far the widest column, so a broad prefix paid for thousands of rows nobody sees. Surfaced when raising the cs-fzf result limit from 20 to 200 made typeahead unusable.
design: Ranking query selects only (msg_id, conv_id, score) and never touches message.text. A hydrate() pass then fetches full rows and builds snippets for the survivors only, via one prepared statement reused across them. Warm, at limit 200: "the" 432ms -> 79ms, "cod" 380ms -> 32ms, "code" 469ms -> 98ms, "rus" 296ms -> 38ms.
notes: The 400-800 ms figures quoted while investigating were cold-cache artifacts from re-running with different arguments; the numbers above are warmed and are the honest comparison.
close_reason: Landed in cs-core/src/search.rs: ranking query drops message.text, hydrate() fetches survivors only. 108 tests passing.

title: Record ADR 14 as decided: no daemon, clients link cs-core or spawn the CLI
description: ADR 14 (subprocess vs daemon) has been open and is listed as blocking client work. Measurements settle it: an in-process query is 1.4-6.4 ms and process spawn plus opening the 293 MB index is ~3 ms, so a daemon buys about 3 ms in exchange for a socket protocol, lifecycle management and cache-staleness bugs. Rust clients link cs-core directly; everything else spawns cs search --json at ~9 ms end to end, which fits a typeahead budget. Needs writing up in DECISIONS.md so the decision is not re-litigated.
close_reason:
Done, verified. docs/DECISIONS.md:210 now carries '## 14. Client seam: no daemon — link the core in Rust, spawn the CLI elsewhere', accepted 2026-07-29, in full house style: Context with a measurement table, three Options (resident daemon / link-and-spawn / C-ABI shared library) with honest Pro-Con bullets, Decision, Why, and a Revisit-when. Option A states real advantages rather than a strawman — per-keystroke rather than per-session saving, the only home for cross-query state, and single-writer ownership if incremental indexing lands — and its decisive con is the ADR 1 interaction: a rebuild deletes and recreates index.db, so a daemon holding an open handle reads a deleted inode and serves stale results silently. Also fixes the stale cross-reference under ADR 12 (line 179), which pointed at '(see 13)' when it always meant 14. ADR 15 (redaction) is now the only 'open' entry in the file; ADRs 9-12 remain 'proposed'.

Two corrections applied on review, both unsourced numbers the draft had stated as project constraints: a '~50 ms keystroke-to-paint budget' and a derived '~40 ms of headroom' appeared nowhere else in the repo, and the Context line claimed the figures were measured 'against the real 293 MB index, not the PoC corpus' — a provenance the repo does not record. BACKLOG.md:94 and this bead give the 1.4-6.4 ms / ~3 ms figures without stating where they were taken, and poc/RESULTS.md has different numbers (rust --release 3.8 ms mean, 4.9 ms p95). Softened to 'fits a type-ahead budget' (matching BACKLOG.md:57's existing unquantified phrasing) and to 'the measurements this was decided against, recorded 2026-07-29'. The ~20 ms revisit trigger was rewritten to anchor on today's ~3 ms rather than on the invented budget.

title: Decide redaction: at import or at display (ADR 15)
description:
The location half of this bead was split out on 2026-08-01 as chat-search-4ar.6, which is mechanical and actionable today. What remains here is the decision, and it is ADR 15's, not a task's.

ADR 15 is `open`. Its context: agent transcripts contain env vars, tokens and file contents, and the index concentrates all of it into one file. Not yet decided is whether to redact at import — destructive, and in tension with ADR 1 unless the raw archive is kept intact — or at display, which is safer for reparse but leaves the index holding secrets on disk.

ADR 15's own 'decide by' is the honest trigger: before any surface is shared, or any archive leaves this machine. Neither has happened. It does, however, block real work — a7k.15 (encrypted offsite tier) is gated on it outright, since an offsite copy IS the archive leaving this machine.

Kept open rather than deferred, because unlike the other gated beads this one is not waiting on a threshold or on a second machine. It is waiting on a decision that can be made at any time, and making it early is cheap while making it late is not: every month of transcripts captured under an undecided policy is a month that a redact-at-import answer cannot retroactively apply to without a reparse.
acceptance_criteria:
ADR 15 moves off `open` in docs/DECISIONS.md, with the choice recorded and its consequence for ADR 1 stated explicitly — if redaction happens at import, the doc has to say what 'raw is the source of truth' now means when raw has been altered, or say that raw is kept unredacted and only the derived index is scrubbed.

docs/BACKLOG.md's 'Decisions still open' table drops the ADR 15 row.

Whatever is decided is written down as a rule with one home, not as a policy each importer or client re-implements. If it is redact-at-display, the redactor is in cs-core where every client reaches it; if at import, it is a documented stage in the importer contract, which ADR 1 requires to stay a pure function of (logical_path, bytes).

chat-search-a7k.15 is named in the outcome either way, since it is blocked on this.
notes:
Changed shape on 2026-07-30. Until now everything under archive_root was either re-derivable from the source tools (raw/) or disposable (index.db), so losing the archive cost time rather than data. ~/.chat-archive/queries.jsonl is neither: it records what was searched for and what was opened, and nothing can reconstruct it.

Two consequences for this issue:
- Backup is now load-bearing for one specific file, not merely nice to have.
- Redaction gets a new surface. Query text is a direct record of what was being worked on and worried about, in a way transcripts only imply — arguably the most sensitive per byte of anything here. Any 'sync the archive somewhere' answer has to decide about this file specifically.
- 'log_queries = false' in config is the opt-out if the conclusion is that it should not exist on a synced machine.

title: Quick surface — Raycast
description: Raycast first to validate ranking before investing in chrome. ~200 lines of TypeScript shelling out to the binary, whose 4.9 ms p95 cold start fits a type-ahead budget.
acceptance_criteria:
A Raycast extension searches the index and opens a chosen conversation, shelling out to `cs search --json` rather than linking or reimplementing anything. No Rust changes are needed to make it work — if any turn out to be, that is a finding about ADR 12's contract and belongs in its own bead.

It consumes `destinations` as structured data and picks a variant, rather than parsing a rendered string (ADR 12; me9.3 is what made this possible). A result whose destinations list is empty renders as un-openable rather than as a broken command.

Typing stays inside a type-ahead budget end to end, measured through the extension rather than assumed from the binary's 4.9 ms cold start. State the measured p95 for a keystroke, and say which queries were used — broad prefixes are the ones that hurt (6eb.29).

It records picks. `cs pick <conv_id> --query <text>` exists precisely so a client's selection feeds the query log, and a client that opens conversations without recording which one was chosen throws away the ground truth 6eb.21 needs.

The point is validating ranking before investing in chrome, so the outcome includes a judgement: after real use, does the ranking hold up? That answer is the deliverable, not the extension.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. Unblocked as of me9.3 — docs/BACKLOG.md's ordering trap 4 ('query contract before client #2') is recorded as met, because destinations replaced the single pre-rendered resume_cmd string.

Contract as it stands today, verified 2026-08-01 against the real index, so the extension knows what it is consuming:
  top level  count, grouped, ms, query, results, unapplied_filters
  result     conv_id, native_id, source, title, cwd, ended_at, ended_date, user_turns,
             msg_count, prose_count, score, match_count, match_seqs, hits, destinations,
             deleted_upstream
  destination  { kind: "terminal", argv: ["claude", "--resume", "<id>"] }

argv is a vector, not a shell string, which is the detail a TypeScript client most easily gets wrong — spawn it directly rather than joining and passing to a shell, or a cwd with a space in it breaks the open. The bd memory on crossterm and inherited descriptors is the same lesson in the other direction.

Note only kind 'terminal' is emitted at present. The AC's empty-destinations case is therefore about future sources (chatgpt-export has no local resume), not a hypothetical.

title: Never render an empty successful search on failure
description: Keep the previous results and show the error. An empty result list reads as "nothing matched", which is a lie when the real answer is "the reader failed to reload".
acceptance_criteria:
A test proves that a search failure leaves the previous result set on screen and reports the error, rather than rendering an empty list. That is the whole of the remaining work — the behaviour itself already landed.

The test must fail if the Err arm is changed to clear self.groups, which is the specific regression worth guarding: the failure mode is silent and looks exactly like a successful search that matched nothing, so nothing else would catch it.

Cover the two layers separately, since they are two different lies: state.rs must keep the groups, and render.rs must say 'search failed' rather than 'no results'.
notes:
ASSESSED 2026-08-01: the behaviour is implemented, the proof is not.

Already done, and citing this bead by name in the source:
  crates/cs-tui/src/state.rs:110-143 — the Err arm sets self.status and leaves self.groups untouched
  crates/cs-tui/src/render.rs:161  — 'search failed — showing nothing rather than guessing'
  crates/cs-tui/src/render.rs:380  — the same rule one layer down, for an empty message list

Not a concern on the CLI: cs search propagates the error with ? and exits non-zero, so it cannot render an empty success by construction.

What is missing is a test. Nothing in crates/cs-tui pins any of it, so the guarantee currently rests on three comments. Scoped the bead to that rather than closing it, because a rule this easy to regress silently is exactly the kind that needs the test more than the comment.

title: Generation-numbered searches
description: Each keystroke query carries an incrementing number; results from an older generation are dropped on arrival. Without it a slow query that started three keystrokes ago overwrites the fresh results with stale ones. fast-resume tui/state.rs carries both a search_generation and an applied_search_generation so it can also tell "in flight" from "settled". NOTE: the native TUI issue argues the opposite — that at 6 ms the search is synchronous and no generation counter is needed. Resolve the contradiction before building either.
close_reason: Superseded by chat-search-me9.1's design. A generation counter exists to discard results from a query that is still in flight when a newer keystroke arrives. Our search is synchronous in the event loop at 1.4-6.4 ms, so there is never an in-flight query to go stale and the counter guards nothing. fast-resume needs search_generation and applied_search_generation because Tantivy plus a background rescan is genuinely async; we are not. Reinstate trigger recorded on me9.1: if any keystroke path exceeds ~30 ms — most likely via the query DSL (chat-search-6eb.11) or fuzzy-on-failure (chat-search-6eb.10) — the search stops being synchronous and this comes back.

title: CLI search rebuilt against the real schema
description: The PoC has one; it needs rebuilding against the real schema.
close_reason: Already done. cs search is built against the real schema — grouped output, the 6eb.11 filter DSL, me9.3 destinations, and --json as the ADR 12 client contract. The description ('the PoC has one; it needs rebuilding') describes a state that ended when the real CLI landed. Verified 2026-08-01: ./target/release/cs search returns grouped, ranked, dated results off index.db.

title: Tune REPEAT_WEIGHT and the decay constant against a real eval set
description: REPEAT_WEIGHT is currently 0.25.
design:
Now a shell loop rather than a rebuild. REPEAT_WEIGHT and DECAY are per-query fields on cs_core::Query (defaults unchanged), and 'cs eval run' takes --repeat-weight and --decay, so:

  for w in 0.0 0.15 0.25 0.4 1.0; do
    cs eval run --set evals/ranking.toml --repeat-weight $w --json |
      jq -r '"$w \(.report.ndcg) \(.report.mrr)"'
  done

Two traps, both already guarded:
- Judge before sweeping. A sweep over a thin pool measures the pool. 'cs eval run' warns below 80% coverage.
- The judging pool already spans decay=0 and repeat_weight=0 rankers, so a conversation the current constants bury is still a judging candidate. Without that, any sweep would conclude the current values are optimal by construction.
notes:
Re-gated 2026-07-30 on chat-search-6eb.21 rather than the deferred chat-search-6eb.9. Removing the old edge briefly left this in 'bd ready' with nothing to tune against, which is precisely the failure the eval exists to prevent — a sweep with no eval set reports numbers that are entirely a function of which results happened to get judged.

Also note the overlap with chat-search-6eb.12: that issue proposes removing the recency decay altogether rather than tuning it, on the grounds that fast-resume applies none. If 6eb.12 wins, half of this issue disappears. Decide 6eb.12 first, or at least measure both in the same sweep.

title: Never let a worse parse overwrite a better one
description: fast-resume classifies a JSONL file as clean / partial / invalid and retains the previously indexed document rather than replacing it from a truncated read. We are insulated from the worst case because the archive holds the bytes, but a mid-write scan still yields a half conversation until the next run.
design: Cheap to adopt: Clean | Partial | Invalid, keyed on whether any valid record follows the last malformed one.
acceptance_criteria:
A scan that reads a file mid-write does not replace a good indexed conversation with a truncated one. The test is the one that reproduces the bug: index a complete transcript, then index a deliberately truncated copy of it, and assert the complete conversation survives.

Each file is classified Clean | Partial | Invalid on the rule already in the design — whether any valid record follows the last malformed one — and the classification is visible in `cs index` output rather than being an internal detail, so a run that read a file mid-write says so.

A Partial read never overwrites a Clean one for the same conversation. A Partial read DOES land when there is nothing indexed for that conversation yet, since half a conversation beats none.

This holds across runs without extra state: the archive holds the bytes (ADR 1), so a later run that reads the same file complete replaces the partial one and the index converges. Nothing needs to remember that a previous read was partial — it only needs to not lose to one.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. The design was already recorded; what was missing is the precedence rule, which is where this class of change goes wrong. 'Retain the previously indexed document' is ambiguous about the first-ever read, and the answer differs: partial-over-nothing is an improvement, partial-over-complete is the bug.

The description is right that the archive insulates us from the worst case — bytes are never lost — so this is about the window between a mid-write capture and the next run, not about permanent corruption. That bounds the priority: the damage is temporary and self-healing, which is why it is P2 and not P1.

title: Codex fork replay dedup
description: A fork copies the parent whole transcript into the child file, so fork-heavy projects flood results with near-identical hits.
acceptance_criteria:
A fork and its parent no longer return as near-identical separate hits for the same query. The measurement is a before/after on a fork-heavy project in the real corpus: state how many duplicate-looking conversations a representative query returned before, and what it returns after.

Replayed content is identified by content, not by file — a fork copies the parent transcript into the child file, so the messages are byte-identical and are detectable as such without trusting any id the format may or may not carry.

Dedup happens at import into the DAG, not in the ranker. ADR 4 makes a conversation a DAG and ADR 7 requires determinism; a ranker-side filter would have to re-derive the relationship on every query and would leave the index still holding the duplicate rows.

Nothing is lost that is not genuinely a replay: the fork's own divergent messages — everything after the branch point — remain searchable and attributed to the fork. The failure to avoid is collapsing a fork whose later content is the thing being searched for.

A test builds a parent and a fork sharing a prefix and asserts one conversation's worth of shared messages, both branches' tails intact.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. Related but distinct from ADR 7's dedup, which handles a conversation spanning several transcript files (the bug that made IndexStats double-count 69 conversations). This is the opposite shape: one logical history copied into two files by a fork.

Check first whether search_grouped's grouping already hides some of this — it collapses a conversation's hits into one row, so the visible symptom may be N sibling conversations rather than N rows of one. That changes what 'flood results' means and therefore what the fix has to do.

title: Claude Code queued_command attachments
description: Real user prompts typed while a tool ran. No uuid/parentUuid, so they must be spliced by timestamp; currently dropped.
acceptance_criteria:
A queued_command attachment reaches the index as a user message with the prose the user actually typed, rather than being dropped.

It is spliced into the DAG by timestamp, and the test that matters covers the ambiguous case: two queued commands typed while the same tool ran must land in typed order, not in an order that depends on HashMap iteration or file order. ADR 7's determinism rule applies — the same bytes must produce the same DAG on every run.

A spliced message is distinguishable from one that carried its own uuid, so a later importer that gains real ids can tell what it inferred from what it was told. Splicing by timestamp is a heuristic and the index should not forget which of its edges were guessed.

The count is stated: how many messages this recovers across the corpus, measured before and after, so the change is justified by what it recovers rather than by the fact that it parses.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. The description already states the mechanism (no uuid/parentUuid, so splice by timestamp) — what it did not state is the determinism constraint, which is the part most likely to be got wrong and the one ADR 7 exists for.

Worth measuring first: 'real user prompts typed while a tool ran' is a claim about how much genuine authored text is being lost, and that number decides the priority. If it is a handful of messages the bead is cosmetic; if it is hundreds it is a recall bug in the most valuable class of message the corpus has, since a user prompt is the thing people search for.

title: Gemini CLI importer
description: 34 files are archived and currently index to zero conversations.
close_reason:
Done, verified. New crates/cs-import/src/gemini.rs, one line in cs-import/src/lib.rs, one match arm in query.rs — scope held exactly. gemini-cli went from 0 conversations to 12, from 15 chats/ files, 120 messages indexed. Re-parenting is implemented correctly against the hazard in Message::parent_native_id: the empty-turn skip happens before prev_native_id advances, so a dropped turn never becomes a parent and no edge dangles.

Corrected two counts in the spec I gave it, both verified against the archive: there are 15 chats/session-*.json files (not 13) and 15 checkpoints (not 17); logs.json at 4 and the 34 total were right. The extra chats files are byte-for-byte duplicates — a personal-site/ directory repeats 3 sessions already present under a hash directory, confirmed by shasum (3 hashes appear exactly twice among the 15).

That duplication drove a design call worth keeping: message native_id is the record's own UUID rather than a per-file ordinal, so the index's INSERT OR IGNORE folds the second copy instead of doubling the conversation. model.rs sanctions this — it asks for file-scoped ids only where the source's own id is file-unique, and Gemini's is a UUID. An ordinal fallback covers a missing or repeated id, which would otherwise be swallowed silently by that same INSERT OR IGNORE.

Also found that 'type' is not only user/gemini — 'info' appears 4 times (auth chatter) and one whole session is nothing but info, so dropping the unknown type would have erased a conversation. Mapped to Role::System and kept. Content is not always a string (2 records are arrays of {text} parts, flattened). Records carry model, now populated last-wins.

13 tests added, all synthetic, covering the four required cases plus unknown type, content-parts flattening, double-archive idempotency, id fallback, model last-wins, and declining logs.json/checkpoints by shape rather than by path. cargo test --workspace: 134 passed, 0 failed, 3 ignored — 119 baseline + 3 (a7k.6) + 12. Follow-ups filed as chat-search-n58.21 (thoughts as Reasoning, 118 of 152 messages carry it) and chat-search-n58.22 (logs.json is not purely redundant — session 74eb0b66 has no chats/ file and survives only there).

title: 8 Codex subagent files cannot be linked to their parent
description: Older rollouts carry neither session_id nor parent_thread_id, so they surface as standalone conversations. Recovering them needs a cross-file pass.
acceptance_criteria:
The 8 orphaned Codex subagent files are linked to their parent conversation, or the bead records why a specific file cannot be and that file is left standalone deliberately. Either outcome is acceptable; a silent partial fix is not — state the count linked out of 8.

Linking survives a full reparse. The cross-file pass runs inside the importer stage over the archive, so `rm index.db && cs index` reproduces the same links (ADR 1, ADR 7). A one-off repair script that mutates the index is the wrong shape — it makes the index no longer a pure function of the archive.

A subagent linked by inference is distinguishable from one linked by an id the file carried, so a later format change that restores session_id does not silently inherit guesses as facts.

A test covers the negative: two unrelated standalone rollouts that merely look similar must NOT be linked. Recovering 8 files is not worth inventing a parent for a 9th.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. The description gives the cause (older rollouts carry neither session_id nor parent_thread_id) but not the recovery signal, which is the actual design question and should be settled before anyone starts: what identifies a parent when both ids are absent? Candidates visible in the corpus are the cwd plus an overlapping time window, and a first-message match against a tool call in the parent.

Worth pricing before doing: 8 files against a 3,003-conversation corpus is 0.27%. The reason to do it anyway is that a subagent surfacing standalone is a wrong answer rather than a missing one — it shows up as a conversation that appears to start mid-task with no context.

title: Codex legacy pre-payload format
description:
18 of the 692 archived Codex files (2.6%) predate the `payload` wrapper, and 121 prose
messages across 17 conversations are silently dropped today.

Verified against the archive on 2026-07-29, not inferred. Every `.jsonl` under `codex/` was
scanned: exactly 18 carry no `payload` key on any line and no `event_msg` anywhere. They are
**one** format, not several — chat-search-n58.16 filed the same 18 files under a
"pre-2025-09-09" boundary and was closed as a duplicate.

Shape:

- Line 1 is a session header: `{id, timestamp, instructions, git{commit_hash, branch, repository_url}}`.
- Every later line is either a bare Responses-API item — `type` of `message` (carrying
  `role` and `content`), `reasoning`, `function_call`, `function_call_output` — or the
  separator line `{"record_type":"state"}`.

The range is 2025-08-07 to 2025-12-07, so this format outlived the date any single cutover
would suggest. Recoverable prose is 58 user + 63 assistant = 121 messages across 17 files.
The 18th (`2025/08/07/rollout-2025-08-07T16-54-05-2df3f3be…jsonl`) is a header-only stub with
no messages at all — a useful edge case for the parser not to choke on.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `cs index`
2. Query for text known to be in one of the 18 files, e.g. from
   `2025/12/07/rollout-2025-12-07T17-19-51-eff5d92b…jsonl`.
3. Zero hits. The file was read and produced no messages; nothing reports that it was skipped.
design: Needs a disjoint code path gated on 'line has no payload object', which cannot regress the current format. Detect on the header line rather than per-message: line 1 having id+timestamp+git and no payload is an unambiguous format marker, so the file is classified once and dispatched, instead of every line paying a branch. The item shapes are plain Responses-API objects, so the message/reasoning/function_call mapping to Kind is the same table the current parser already has — only the unwrapping differs. Zero event_msg means there is no turn-boundary signal at all: seq comes from line order.
acceptance_criteria: All 18 legacy files import without error. 121 prose messages (58 user, 63 assistant) are indexed across 17 conversations. The header-only 2025-08-07 file yields no conversation rather than an error or an empty-titled row. The 674 payload-format files produce byte-identical index output to before the change, proven by a full reindex diff. Synthetic fixtures only — no real transcripts in the repo (chat-search-4ar.3).

title: Watch vs scan
description: Decides archiver latency and whether a daemon is needed.
close_reason: Answered by shipping. The archiver has run under launchd at 300 s since chat-search-a7k.2 and the latency is fine in practice; no daemon was needed. Nothing in the bead said what would reopen the question, so it was a spike with no live decision behind it. Refile with a concrete trigger (e.g. a source whose writes must be captured in under 300 s) if watch ever becomes worth its complexity.

title: Decompress .zst rollouts in the Codex importer
description: The archiver now captures them verbatim, but nothing can read them yet. Latent until Codex starts compressing here.
acceptance_criteria:
A .zst rollout in the archive imports to the same conversations and messages the equivalent uncompressed rollout produces. A golden test asserts that equivalence directly — same file, compressed and not, must yield byte-identical importer output — since that is the only way to prove decompression is transparent rather than merely non-crashing.

Decompression happens inside the importer, not the archiver. ADR 1 requires the archive to hold source bytes verbatim, and the importer contract is a pure function of (logical_path, bytes), so the bytes it receives are the compressed ones and it decompresses in memory.

A truncated or corrupt .zst is declined the way any unparseable file is declined — it is reported, and it does not abort the run or take the rest of the source down with it.

Selection is by content, not by filename: a rollout that is compressed without a .zst suffix, or named .zst without being compressed, must not silently import as empty.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. Still latent — nothing in the current archive is compressed; the trigger is Codex starting to compress rollouts, at which point every new file silently imports as zero messages if this is not in.

Note the new dependency. The workspace has no zstd crate today (rusqlite, serde, serde_json, toml, thiserror, anyhow, blake3, globset, reflink-copy, uuid, clap, chrono, chrono-tz, ratatui, unicode-width), so this adds one to a deliberately small set. ADR 20 already measured zstd on this corpus at 2.98-3.13x for rollouts, so the format is not in question — only the dependency is.

The silent-empty failure is the one worth designing against: an importer that declines a file it cannot read produces a source that contributes nothing, and cs index already has a row for that case (a7k.22's work). Make sure a compressed file lands in that reporting path rather than in the 'parsed fine, zero messages' path, which looks like an empty transcript.

title: Claude.ai capture
description:
SUPERSEDED — kept for the record because its one-line premise was half wrong.

Original text: 'No local files at all; needs export or API.'

What a survey of this machine on 2026-07-30 actually found:
- 'No local files at all' is false for the Claude DESKTOP app. Cowork and Chat tab transcripts sit in the clear at ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/local-agent-mode-sessions/ — 14 sessions, 30 MB. title: bytes captured overstates disk cost
description: An append re-clones the whole file, so the reported figure is file size, not delta. Report allocated blocks instead.
close_reason:
Done, verified — but the bead's prescribed fix turned out not to be what closes the honesty gap, and that is worth recording. scan.rs gained allocated_bytes(&Metadata) (cfg(unix): blocks()*512; cfg(not(unix)): len()) filled from the existing stat call, so no second syscall; FileChange carries it on all paths including the Unchanged fast path. main.rs replaced three loose counters with a Bytes{apparent, allocated, cloned, copied} struct. capture.rs needed no edit — CaptureKind already carried the clone-vs-copy split. JSON contract preserved: 'bytes' and 'bytes_to_capture' keep their exact prior values and meaning; apparent_bytes, allocated_bytes, cloned_bytes, copied_bytes, allocated_to_capture were added alongside. cargo test -p cs-archive 36 passed 0 failed (33 baseline + 3).

FINDING, independently verified: allocated blocks does NOT reduce the figure. Measured over the real 1057-file archive, allocated/apparent is 1.0010 (2268.2 MB vs 2270.4 MB) — these transcripts are neither sparse nor compressed, so blocks()*512 is len() rounded up to 4 KB. Also confirmed by direct experiment that an APFS clonefile destination reports the source's full st_blocks (both 1528 blocks / 782336 bytes for a 780000-byte file), so no stat-based figure can observe the block sharing at all. The clone/copy split from CaptureKind is therefore the only thing that expresses real marginal cost, and on this machine every capture clones, so the report now honestly reads '0.0 MB new on disk' where it used to read '0.7 MB captured'.

The dominant error — an append re-billing the whole file every 300 s — is now visible but not removed. Tracked as a follow-up.
